newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines allows peso to move, IMF applauds plan.
newsitem.headline: Philippines allows peso to move, IMF applauds plan.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank said on Friday that it would allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar, a move traders said amounted to the second de facto devaluation of an Asian currency this month.
The peso slumped to 29.45 to the U.S. dollar soon after the announcement from Thursday's close of 26.40. The Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) later temporarily halted peso-dollar trades.
"Starting today....(the central bank) will allow the peso-U.S. dollar rate to move within a new wider range consistent with significantly changed market conditions," the bank said in a statement.

"This is expected to remove the incentive for speculation against the peso and allow a gradual reduction in interest rates more compatible with the economy's requirements for sustainable economic growth," the bank said.
The bank gave no indication of what the wider rate would be.
"(The bank) remains fully committed to the market-oriented exchange rate arrangement which has served the Philippines well," it said.

"While the underlying exchange rate policy will remain unchanged, (the Central Bank) will allow greater flexibility in the peso-U.S. dollar rate. This is being taken to facilitate more timely adjustment in light of more difficult conditions in regional currency markets," the statement said.
It added that the move would be done in the context of continued prudent macro-economic policies.
Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson was due to give a news conference on Friday at 10 a.m. (0200 GMT).
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said he welcomed the action by the Philippines Central Bank to allow greater exchange rate flexibility.

In a statement issued in Washington, Camdessus also said he would recommend that the IMF board approve the Philippines' request for an extension of its Extended Fund Facility and said he would ask the board to make additional borrowing authority available.
"The management of the IMF strongly commends the Philippine authorities for their timely and decisive action," Camdessus said.

"I am confident that this set of measures, in conjunction with the authorities' resolve to maintain fiscal and monetary discipline, will help protect the Philippine economy from the consequences of instability in regional financial markets," Camdessus said.
The country's foreign exchange reserves have been depleted by repeated intervention, and interest rates raised to levels which could hurt the economy.

Although the government has so far steadfastly declined to say how much money it has left in its kitty, official figures last put foreign exchange reserves at just under $12 billion in May -- a bit more than three months' worth of imports.
The peso is the latest victim of regional currency speculation.
Earlier this month authorities in Thailand announced a managed float of the baht. The baht lost 15 to 20 p ercent of its value after the move.
